For instance, barhä [baɽá] f. 'daughter' vs. barha [báɽa] m. 'son'. ... [sec.4, p.7] The subjunctive is always stressed on the penultimate syllable, and should not be confused with the jussive, which is stressed on the final syllable and is used mainly for wishes and commands ... [sec.5.2, p.9] There are two genders: masculine (m.) and feminine (f.). audit.reasoning: Quote check passes: the deciding B&V 2005 passages are verbatim at the stated PDF pages in the copy we hold. The classification (contrastive, morphologically placed pitch accent on penult/final; tonal-OR-pitch accent, not weight-sensitive, right edge, word domain) is independently stated by the held 370-pp reference grammar (Esayas 2015 sec. 2.2.3: tone-accent, H restricted to final or penultimate mora, lexical + grammatical, unaccented words) and by three sources downloaded now: Welmers 1952:147 primary text (lexical + morphological 'stress' realized as highest pitch, many stems unaccented), B&V 2010 EAE p.469 (summarizing Hayward 1997: pitch accent, one tone-bearing syllable per word, NP sandhi) and B&V 2017 p.68 (m. H-L vs f. L-H). Nothing ties accent to syllable weight in any of them. The only unheld tone-specific works (Hayward 1983, 1997) are print-only and, per the authors who cite them

sources.citation: Welmers, William E. (1952). Notes on the structure of Saho. Word 8: 145-162, 236-251.

sources.quote: 'Stress in different positions is obviously the determining factor in contrasts such as those between |yibáda| my son and |yibadá| my daughter ... the stressed vowel has the highest pitch, and the form ends with low pitch. But forms that are not clearly stressed on a vowel before the last one are pronounced in isolation with a final high pitch ... may also be interpreted as conditioned by an absence of stress in the form ... forms with fewer than two stresses are interpreted as having either stress with a vowel other than the last, or no stress ... stress has both a lexical and a morphological

sources.quote: 'Hayward (1997: 69ff.) describes central and southern S. varieties as having a system of pitch accent with either high or low tones on short vowels and also falling and rising tones on long vowels. Only one syllable generally bears a high, falling or rising tone in each word, and tonal sandhi operates within complex noun phrases (NPs).'

sources.note: The one dedicated treatment of Saho tone/pitch accent (H/L on short vowels, contour tones on long vowels, one accent per word, NP tonal sandhi), cited by the second reader&V 2010 as the description of the system; would supply a primary phonological statement of culminativity and accentless words to replace the 1952 Welmers secondary.
